title: The Self-Reinforcing Urn
statement: An urn starts with one red and one blue ball. Ten times, you draw a ball at random, then return it along with one extra ball of the same color. What is the probability that exactly $5$ of the $10$ draws were red?
insight: Any specific sequence with k reds has the same probability k!(10−k)!/11!, so the number of reds is uniform on 0..10.
redHerring: Tracking the urn draw by draw with a large probability tree.
hints: Compute the probability of a specific sequence, say RRB. Then try RBR.
The numerators multiply $1\cdot2\cdots$ for reds and $1\cdot2\cdots$ for blues, in whatever order they come.
So every sequence with $k$ reds has probability $\tfrac{k!(10-k)!}{11!}$. Multiply by the number of such sequences.
solution:
For any sequence with $k$ reds and $10-k$ blues, the denominators are $2,3,\dots,11$ and the numerators are $1,2,\dots,k$ for reds and $1,2,\dots,10-k$ for blues. So the probability is $\tfrac{k!(10-k)!}{11!}$ regardless of order.

$P(k \text{ reds}) = \binom{10}{k}\tfrac{k!(10-k)!}{11!} = \tfrac{10!}{11!} = \tfrac1{11}$ for every $k$.
